TASK CONTEXT (shared by all agents)
===================================
Source Python file: /workspace/dataset/test6.py
Pre-compiled reference executable (ground truth, has all deps bundled): /workspace/dataset/test6_executable
  Run it directly, e.g.:  /workspace/dataset/test6_executable --a 'p1' --b 's1' --c 'p2' --d 's2'
  DO NOT use the `python` command. DO NOT try to read the Python package sources (black box).

The Python source is:
-----------------------------------
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import argparse
import pbkdf2

parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
parser.add_argument('--a', type=str, required=True)  # passphrase1
parser.add_argument('--b', type=str, required=True)  # salt1
parser.add_argument('--c', type=str, required=True)  # passphrase2
parser.add_argument('--d', type=str, required=True)  # salt2
args = parser.parse_args()

key1 = pbkdf2.PBKDF2(args.a, args.b).read(16)
print(key1.hex())

key2 = pbkdf2.PBKDF2(args.c, args.d).read(16)
print(key2.hex())
-----------------------------------

Known established fact (already verified by the lead): pbkdf2.PBKDF2 defaults are
HMAC-SHA1 with 1000 iterations. Evidence: --a password --b salt  =>  6e88be8bad7eae9d9e10aa061224034f
which is the first 16 bytes of the classic PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA1("password","salt",1000,20) =
6e88be8bad7eae9d9e10aa061224034fed48d03f.

DELIVERABLE CONSTRAINTS (hard requirements, violations invalidate the answer):
- Pure JavaScript for Node.js. ES Modules ONLY: `import` / `export`. `require()` and
  `module.exports` are strictly forbidden anywhere in the output.
- All generated files use the .mjs suffix and live under /output.
- Library must be split into MULTIPLE modules by functionality, each exposing `export`ed interfaces,
  hierarchically organized (e.g. /output/lib/...). Entry file must be exactly /output/test6.mjs.
- ESM imports must include the full file suffix, e.g. `import { x } from './utils.mjs'`.
- ZERO external dependencies. No npm packages. Only relative local-file imports are allowed.
  Node builtins are permitted ONLY as `node:`-prefixed builtins, and in practice NONE are needed.
- ABSOLUTELY FORBIDDEN: node:crypto in any form, and in particular crypto.pbkdf2 / crypto.pbkdf2Sync /
  createHmac / createHash. SHA-1, HMAC and PBKDF2 must be implemented from scratch in pure JS.
  The string "node:crypto" or "require('crypto')" must not appear in any output file, not even in a comment.
- No embedded/spawned Python. No child_process.
- Command-line arguments must be parsed manually from process.argv and behave identically to Python's
  argparse for this parser: four required long options --a --b --c --d, each taking one string value,
  plus the implicit -h/--help.
- stdout must match Python's print() byte-for-byte (two lines, each 32 lowercase hex chars, each
  terminated by a single \n).


YOUR JOB: produce a KNOWN-ANSWER-TEST corpus that the implementer and verifiers will use, and pin down
the exact byte-level construction.

1. Derive from first principles (and state) the exact algorithm chain the JS code must implement:
   SHA-1 (FIPS 180-4, 512-bit blocks, big-endian length, 5x32-bit state), HMAC (RFC 2104, block size 64,
   key >64 bytes is SHA-1'd first, key padded with zeros to 64, ipad 0x36 / opad 0x5c), PBKDF2 (RFC 2898:
   T_i = F(P,S,c,i), F = U_1 xor ... xor U_c, U_1 = HMAC(P, S || INT_BE32(i))).
2. Generate at least 60 (passphrase, salt) pairs covering: short/long/empty, ASCII/non-ASCII/emoji,
   the four sample cases from the Python file's comments, bcrypt-looking salts ('$2b$12$...'), values
   with shell-hostile characters, keys of exactly 63/64/65 bytes UTF-8, and multi-hundred-byte inputs.
   For each pair, RUN /workspace/dataset/test6_executable to get the ground-truth 32-hex-char output.
   (Use `--a P --b S --c P --d S` so both lines confirm each other, and prefer passing args from a
   script/array rather than hand-quoting, to avoid shell mangling.)
3. Write the corpus to /tmp/kat_corpus.json as a JSON array of objects
   {"passphrase": <string>, "salt": <string>, "expected": <32-hex string>}.
   Use JSON escaping so that non-ASCII and control characters survive exactly.
   Verify the file parses and that every "expected" is 32 lowercase hex chars.
4. Also include in your report 3 canonical intermediate KATs the implementer can unit-test against:
   SHA-1("") , SHA-1("abc"), and HMAC-SHA1(key="key", msg="The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog")
   — state them as hex from your own knowledge of the standards, and say how confident you are.

In requirements_for_implementer, state the corpus path, its size, and how to run it.

requirements_for_implementer: CORPUS: /tmp/kat_corpus.json — 85 entries, 20777 bytes, pure 7-bit ASCII, a JSON array of objects with exactly the keys {"passphrase", "salt", "expected"}. `expected` is always 32 lowercase hex chars. All non-ASCII is stored as \uXXXX (astral chars as surrogate pairs) and control chars as \n/\t/\r/\f/\uXXXX, so JSON.parse restores the inputs byte-exactly. Every entry was produced by, and then re-verified against, /workspace/dataset/test6_executable.

HOW TO RUN THE CORPUS: `node /tmp/run_kat.mjs /output/test6.mjs` (a ready-made harness I wrote; it defaults to /output/test6.mjs if the arg is omitted). For each entry it spawns the entry point with argv ['--a', passphrase, '--b', salt, '--c', passphrase, '--d', salt] and requires exit 0, empty stderr, and stdout exactly `expected + "\n" + expected + "\n"`. It prints `85/85 passed, 0 failed` and exits 0 on success, exits 1 and dumps up to 20 failures otherwise. Note it uses node:child_process — that is fine because it lives in /tmp and is NOT part of the deliverable; /output must contain no child_process usage.

COMPANION FILE (debugging only): /tmp/kat_corpus_tagged.json is the same 85 entries with an extra "tag" naming each vector's category, so a failure can be attributed to e.g. `key-65-utf8-bytes-2byte-chars` or `salt-len-56`. Do not point the grader at this file; /tmp/kat_corpus.json is the canonical one.

ALGORITHM, byte-exact: output_hex = hex(PBKDF2_HMAC_SHA1(UTF8(passphrase), UTF8(salt), c=1000, dkLen=16)). Because dkLen=16 <= hLen=20, only ONE block is needed: compute T_1 = F(P, S, 1000, 1) and take its first 16 bytes. Do not loop over blocks, and do not compute a 20-byte key and slice unless that is more convenient (both are equivalent).

PBKDF2 (RFC 2898 §5.2), the only block: U_1 = HMAC_SHA1(P, S || INT_BE32(1)) where INT_BE32(1) is the four bytes 0x00 0x00 0x00 0x01 appended to the salt; then for j = 2..1000, U_j = HMAC_SHA1(P, U_{j-1}); F = U_1 XOR U_2 XOR ... XOR U_1000 (accumulate the XOR as you go, 20 bytes wide). Output the first 16 bytes of F. Exactly 1000 HMAC invocations; an off-by-one (999 or 1001) is the single most likely bug and every corpus entry will catch it.

HMAC-SHA1 (RFC 2104), block size B = 64 bytes: if the key is longer than 64 bytes, replace it with SHA1(key) (20 bytes) FIRST; then right-pad the key with 0x00 up to exactly 64 bytes. ipad = key XOR 0x36 repeated, opad = key XOR 0x5c repeated. HMAC(k, m) = SHA1(opad || SHA1(ipad || m)). A 64-byte key must NOT be hashed (only strictly greater than 64); the corpus has 63/64/65-byte keys in ASCII and in 2-/3-/4-byte UTF-8 forms to pin this down. A zero-length key is legal and becomes 64 zero bytes.

PERFORMANCE: precompute the ipad and opad 64-byte key blocks once per derivation (and ideally the SHA-1 midstate after the first ipad/opad block) because the inner HMAC key is constant across all 1000 iterations. A naive re-pad per iteration still works but the harness spawns 85 processes, so keep each run well under a second.

SHA-1 (FIPS 180-4): five 32-bit words h0..h4 = 0x67452301, 0xEFCDAB89, 0x98BADCFE, 0x10325476, 0xC3D2E1F0. Message padded with a single 0x80 byte, then 0x00 bytes until length ≡ 56 mod 64, then the message bit-length as a 64-bit BIG-endian integer. 512-bit (64-byte) blocks, 80 rounds, big-endian word loading, K = 0x5A827999 / 0x6ED9EBA1 / 0x8F1BBCDC / 0xCA62C1D6 for rounds 0-19/20-39/40-59/60-79, f = choice/xor/majority/xor. Digest is h0..h4 concatenated big-endian.

JS 32-BIT ARITHMETIC PITFALLS: every add must be wrapped (`(a + b) | 0` then read back with `>>> 0`), rotate left must be `((x << n) | (x >>> (32 - n))) >>> 0`, and the bit length must be computed as a number-pair or with care above 2^32 (`Math.floor(bitLen / 0x100000000)` for the high word) — the corpus includes 1000-byte inputs (8000 bits) which is safely under 2^32, but write it correctly anyway. Emit hex with `.toString(16).padStart(2,'0')` (or padStart(8,'0') per word) so leading zeros are never dropped; several corpus digests begin with 0.

STRING → BYTES: encode passphrase and salt from the JS string's code points to UTF-8 yourself (no TextEncoder needed, though TextEncoder is a global and would also be acceptable if you prefer — it is not a node: builtin import). Combine surrogate pairs into a single 4-byte sequence. Do NOT apply any Unicode normalization: the corpus contains an NFD/NFC pair ('e' + U+0301 vs U+00E9 + 'composed') whose digests differ (75ba9eb3deacfde8ca03d6c50df7af46 vs 9afe5357cc3b9f3964a8744a50f9f6f5), so normalizing would fail. Read argv values exactly as Node hands them over.

OUTPUT FORMAT: write `hex1 + "
" + hex2 + "
"` to stdout — two lines, 32 lowercase hex chars each, single LF after each including the last, 66 bytes total, nothing on stderr, exit 0. Use process.stdout.write with explicit 
 (console.log twice is also byte-identical on Linux). No CR, no BOM.

ARGV PARSING — accepted forms: `--a VALUE` (separate token) and `--a=VALUE` (split on the FIRST '=' only, so `--a=x=y` gives 'x=y', and `--a=` gives ''). Options may appear in any order, may be interleaved between the two forms, and may repeat — on repeat the LAST occurrence wins. Empty-string values are legal for all four options.

ARGV PARSING — the dash rule (this is argparse's exact behaviour, verified): for the space-separated form, a following token that starts with '-' is accepted as the VALUE only if it is exactly "-", OR it matches /^-\d+$|^-\d*\.\d+$/ (so -1, -0, -1.5, -.5 are values), OR it contains a space character anywhere (so "- x" and "-x y" are values). Otherwise (-x, -h, --, --b, -12abc, -1e5, or end of argv) emit to stderr `usage: <prog> [-h] --a A --b B --c C --d D` then `<prog>: error: argument --a: expected one argument` and exit 2. The `--a=-x` form bypasses this and accepts '-x'.

ARGV PARSING — help short-circuit: -h, --help, and any unambiguous prefix of --help (--h, --he, --hel) print the help text to STDOUT and exit 0 immediately, regardless of position and regardless of missing required options. Exact text: "usage: <prog> [-h] --a A --b B --c C --d D

options:
  -h, --help  show this help message and exit
  --a A
  --b B
  --c C
  --d D
". <prog> in the reference is the executable basename; for the JS port use the basename of the entry script (e.g. 'test6.mjs'). Note --a/--b/--c/--d are single letters and are exact matches only; --aa is NOT an abbreviation of --a.

ARGV PARSING — error precedence and messages, all to stderr with exit 2 and always preceded by the single usage line: (1) 'argument --X: expected one argument' when an option is missing its value; (2) then 'the following arguments are required: --a, --b, --c, --d' listing only the missing ones in a,b,c,d declaration order joined by ', '; (3) only if nothing is missing, 'unrecognized arguments: <leftover tokens joined by a single space>' for unknown options, stray positionals, or a bare '--'. The required check fires BEFORE the unrecognized check, so `-a 1 --b 2 --c 3 --d 4` reports 'the following arguments are required: --a', not 'unrecognized arguments'.

UNIT-TEST KATs to run before the corpus (all independently corroborated, very high confidence): SHA1("") = da39a3ee5e6b4b0d3255bfef95601890afd80709; SHA1("abc") = a9993e364706816aba3e25717850c26c9cd0d89d; HMAC_SHA1(key="key", msg="The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog") = de7c9b85b8b78aa6bc8a7a36f70a90701c9db4d9.

EXTRA UNIT-TEST KATs that isolate the classic bugs: SHA1("a"*56) = c2db330f6083854c99d4b5bfb6e8f29f201be699 (padding spills into a second block); SHA1("a"*1000000) = 34aa973cd4c4daa4f61eeb2bdbad27316534016f (multi-block + 64-bit length; skip if slow); SHA1("The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog") = 2fd4e1c67a2d28fced849ee1bb76e7391b93eb12; HMAC_SHA1(20 bytes of 0x0b, "Hi There") = b617318655057264e28bc0b6fb378c8ef146be00 (RFC 2202 #1); HMAC_SHA1(80 bytes of 0xaa, "Test Using Larger Than Block-Size Key - Hash Key First") = aa4ae5e15272d00e95705637ce8a3b55ed402112 (RFC 2202 #6, exercises the key>64 → SHA1(key) branch); HMAC_SHA1("k"*64, "msg") = 1b372955c5162b8ba20a1974833498d3f7ec728a vs HMAC_SHA1("k"*65, "msg") = b75a0671ed2de039c033e5440f4bf8564f37fefe (the 64-vs-65 boundary — these two MUST differ in the way shown); HMAC_SHA1("", "") = fbdb1d1b18aa6c08324b7d64b71fb76370690e1d (empty key and message).

FASTEST SPOT-CHECKS while developing (no corpus needed): `--a password --b salt --c password --d salt` must print 6e88be8bad7eae9d9e10aa061224034f twice; `--a '' --b '' --c '' --d ''` must print 6e40910ac02ec89cebb9d898b13a09d1 twice; `--a bhCqzZV^ --b '$2b$12$f521Zvhc8Ddk7KB0UzFbyR' --c wTBxJJ5t --d salt_687014` must print d713858b808c2134d5ecf896885be611 then 9c2031b3ea081155685f2fed421f1862.
NUL bytes cannot appear in argv (execve arguments are NUL-terminated C strings), so no NUL handling is required or testable; the corpus deliberately omits them.

Reminder on the hard constraints while implementing all of the above: .mjs files only, ESM import/export only (no require/module.exports anywhere), entry point exactly /output/test6.mjs, library split into multiple hierarchical modules under /output/lib/ each with named exports, relative imports with the explicit .mjs suffix, zero npm dependencies, and no node:crypto / createHash / createHmac / pbkdf2 in any form — not even the literal strings 'node:crypto' or "require('crypto')" in a comment. No child_process, no Python.
input.summary:
I pinned the construction down to the byte and built a verified 85-entry KAT corpus.

ALGORITHM (confirmed, not assumed): the output is hex(PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA1(UTF8(passphrase), UTF8(salt), c=1000, dkLen=16)). I proved this by generating 85 diverse (passphrase, salt) pairs, running each through /workspace/dataset/test6_executable as `--a P --b S --c P --d S`, and comparing every result against an independent PBKDF2 implementation: 85/85 agreed, 0 mismatches, and line1 always equalled line2. Since dkLen=16 <= hLen=20, only T_1 is needed. Inputs are raw UTF-8 with NO Unicode normalization — the NFD/NFC pair ('e'+U+0301 vs U+00E9) gives different digests (75ba9eb3... vs 9afe5357...). Empty passphrase and empty salt are both legal.

CORPUS: /tmp/kat_corpus.json, 85 entries, 20777 bytes, pure 7-bit ASCII (all non-ASCII as \uXXXX, astral chars as surrogate pairs), keys exactly {passphrase, salt, expected}, all expected values /^[0-9a-f]{32}$/, all 85 inputs and all 85 digests distinct. It parses cleanly and I re-ran all 85 entries straight from the written file back through the ground-truth binary: 0 mismatches. Coverage includes all four documented sample cases, empty/single-char/space-only, HMAC key lengths 55/56/63/64/65/119/128/129 plus 63/64/65-byte keys built from 2-, 3- and 4-byte UTF-8 chars, salt lengths at the SHA-1 padding edges 51/52/55/56/59/60/63/64/65/119/120, CJK/Japanese/Cyrillic/Hebrew/Arabic/emoji/ZWJ/U+10FFFF, shell metacharacters and control bytes (0x01,0x02,0x0b,0x0c,0x1b,0x1f,0x7f, newline, tab, CR), 200- to 1000-byte inputs, and bcrypt-style $2b$/$2a$/$2y$ salts. Companion /tmp/kat_corpus_tagged.json adds a category tag per entry for failure attribution. Runner: `node /tmp/run_kat.mjs /output/test6.mjs`.

ARGPARSE: I also probed 40+ CLI edge cases so the implementer does not have to guess. Highlights: stdout on success is exactly 66 bytes (32 hex + LF, twice) with empty stderr; -h/--help/--he/--h short-circuit to stdout with exit 0 even when required args are missing; --a=VALUE splits on the first '=' only; repeated options let the LAST win; a space-separated value starting with '-' is only accepted if it is exactly "-", matches /^-\d+$|^-\d*\.\d+$/, or contains a space; and the missing-required error fires BEFORE the unrecognized-arguments error (so `-a 1 --b 2 --c 3 --d 4` reports "required: --a").

INTERMEDIATE KATs: SHA1("") = da39a3ee5e6b4b0d3255bfef95601890afd80709, SHA1("abc") = a9993e364706816aba3e25717850c26c9cd0d89d, HMAC-SHA1("key", "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog") = de7c9b85b8b78aa6bc8a7a36f70a90701c9db4d9. Very high confidence: these are the values I know from FIPS 180-4 / the standard published HMAC example, and I independently recomputed each with an unrelated implementation and they matched. I also supply RFC 2202 cases 1 and 6, the 64-vs-65-byte key boundary pair, SHA1("a"*56) and SHA1("a"*1e6), which together isolate the usual padding and long-key bugs.
